records.text: Two facts about identity and ordering inside the authoring workspace. (1) compose::render emits, per prose block, the block's text and — for a paragraph with citations — a `*cites: C…*` marker; the block's own id (P#) is never written into the document. The evidence ledger it appends uses the workspace claim ids verbatim (`ledger_cell(&c.id)`), so a rendered ledger id and a workspace claim id are the same string. (2) claims.rs: ClaimEvent::Create/Revise/Withdraw each carry `timestamp: u64` from workspace::now_unix(), but claims::load_all discards them, exposing only `revisions: usize`. prose.rs's ProseEvent::Create/Revise likewise each carry `timestamp: u64` and load_all discards them, exposing only `revisions: usize`. So both timestamps exist in the shipped jsonl logs and no loader currently surfaces them.

prose.rs lines 41-123: ProseEvent::Create carries id, heading, level, text, cite, before, timestamp: u64; ProseEvent::Revise carries id, text, why, cite: Option<Vec<String>>, timestamp: u64. Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) checks.rs lines 646-760, the in-proof predicate this design reuses verbatim. `current = sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)`; `grading_current` = records for that claim whose `proposition_digest` is empty (grandfathered: "A record with no digest at all predates the field. A claim with no record at all is `ungrounded` — human-owed. The module's stated reason for digest-scoping every one of these: "Every check below asks what the evidence says about *what this claim says now*", and a red that only re-grounding could not clear was rejected as "undischargeable". The loop is defined purely over digests and record membership; no timestamp of any record is read anywhere in it.

(2) facts.rs lines 270-400, `mint_windows` — the one existing check that reasons over timestamps. It reads `FactEvent::Create` timestamps out of the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and refusal timestamps out of `refusals.log`, both written by the same workspace, and it states its own resolution limit rather than hiding it: a refusal whose second equals a mint boundary "cannot be placed on one side of it", so it "appears in both adjacent windows — the same `>=` choice the mint-time replay makes, for the same reason: showing twice is recoverable, hiding once is the incident this exists for." The struct carries `straddles_a_boundary` and report.rs prints the caveat. Its doc also states the standing form for a listing of this class: "The listing is only ever as complete as the log beneath it ... That is not a completeness claim in either direction: a verbatim listing asserts only what was recorded." And the reason it exists at grading time at all: "a line printed at a terminal works only if it is read in the moment, and a memo built on a bad fact otherwise renders and checks clean."

records.text: A whole-worktree grep of /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel for `fn now_unix` finds exactly two definitions: evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257. Both are byte-equivalent — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` — so a prose/claim event timestamp (workspace clock) and an evidence record timestamp (whatever process wrote the record) are the same unit and the same epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What they are not is the same clock: `SystemTime::now()` reads the wall clock of the process that calls it, and nothing in either function or in the record shape ties the two processes together. Note also workspace.rs's separate `ts()` used for refusals.log, which formats the same value as a decimal string.

evidence.rs lines 128-216, the whole record shape. A Statement is {_type, subject: Vec<Subject>, predicateType, predicate}; Subject is {name, digest: DigestSet{sha256}} — one sha256, and it is of the claim proposition; Predicate is {verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, world, note, pin, timestamp}. There is no field anywhere in the record that names or digests a prose block, and RecordInput — the entire ingestion surface a reporter can fill — has no such field either. The only digest a grounding pass writes is over the proposition it was briefed on.

Two observations behind the attack findings.

(1) prose.rs lines 172-202, `revise`: it refuses only on an unknown block id and an empty `--why`. It never compares `new_text` to the block's existing text, and it writes `cite` straight through — so a revision that restates byte-identical text while replacing the citation list is an ordinary, unrefused act. The doc comment says why the `cite` parameter exists: without it "a paragraph created without a citation could never be given one ... which made `tetel review`'s own instruction ('mint the missing claim and cite it') unreachable for existing prose." So a citation-only revision is not merely permitted, it is the act the tool added the parameter to permit.

(2) ledger.rs lines 70-140, `split_row_cells`: it `trim()`s the whole line, un-escapes `\|` back to `|`, respects backtick spans, and `trim()`s every cell it emits. So a ledger cell round-trips a pipe but not leading or trailing whitespace, and — since a markdown row is one physical line — not an embedded newline either.

Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) lib.rs lines 85-100: `check_file` builds its claim list as `ledger::import(&doc.body)` — from the parsed rendered document — and passes exactly those claims to both `checks::analyze` and `checks::analyze_ledger`. So the propositions every `proposition_digest` on record was computed over are the ledger-derived ones, and any check reusing the in-proof predicate must take its claims from `ledger::import`, not from `claims.jsonl`.

Two existing mechanisms that an exclusion disclosure could ride on without a schema change.

(1) compose.rs `render_facts` (lines 205-275 of src/compose.rs): the rendered memo's "## Facts" table has a column "Extent (captured)" whose cell is built by mapping each extent entry to `e.label` and joining with "; ". Its doc comment states explicitly that only the label is rendered, never the `key` (an absolute machine-local path) and never the captured output. So whatever a `look` writes into an extent entry's `label` reaches every reader of the committed memo; whatever it writes anywhere else does not.

(2) facts.rs `mint` (lines 413-437 of src/facts.rs): the pin is sha256 over a string built per pending entry from, in order, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `output`, each newline-terminated. The label is therefore already inside the pin. So a label that names the exclusion set makes two searches with different exclusion sets pin differently even when their matched output is identical.

What happened when it was taken is itself the observation. `look --grep look_grep /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel` succeeded server-side and recorded the search and its per-file hits into the pending buffer, but the agent harness refused to hand the result back, reporting "result (707,751 characters across 38 lines) exceeds maximum allowed tokens" and spilling it to a file instead. So the author of this memo never read the output of their own census; the 38 matched lines were captured, minted and are shipping in this fact's extent and in the snapshot regardless.

That is the return path and the retention path coming apart under measurement. tetel caps neither: observe.rs pushes the whole stdout into `printed` and the whole per-file output into the pending entries. The only cap in the chain was imposed downstream by the harness, on the return path only, and it fired.

The two code sites the exclusion mechanism has to fit between.

(1) src/facts.rs lines 82-103, `ExtentEntry::censuses` — TET-28's census predicate in full. It reads exactly five things: that `kind` is Some(Search) or Some(NoMatch), that `pattern` byte-equals the symbol, that `world_root` is non-empty and not `worldstate::NO_GIT`, and that `key == world_root`. It never reads `label` and never reads `output`. Its doc comment states the predicate "is about existence and rooting, never about what was found".

(2) src/observe.rs lines 158-195, the head of `look_grep`. It refuses a non-existent root, then builds the argument vector: `-r` ONLY when `root_path.is_dir()`, then `-I`, `-n`, `-H`, `-e`, the pattern, and finally `root` — passed through verbatim as the caller spelled it, never canonicalized. `Command::new("grep")` is then invoked with that vector and the whole stdout is taken with `String::from_utf8_lossy`.

src/observe.rs lines 196-258, the tail of `look_grep` — the return path and the retention path, side by side, with no cap on either.

Return path: on a matching search, `printed.push_str(&stdout)` copies the grep's entire stdout into `printed`, and `printed` is what `LookOutcome` carries back to the caller at the end of the function. There is no length check, no truncation, no elision, and no configuration anywhere between the grep's stdout and that return.

Retention path: separately, the same stdout is split by file and each file's matching lines are pushed into a `PendingEntry` whose `output` is `matches.join("\n")` — also uncapped. The whole-search `Search` entry carries `output: String::new()` and a `label` of the form "search: {root} (grep: {pattern}) — {files} file(s) matched"; the zero-match `NoMatch` entry likewise carries empty output and a "no-match: {pattern} in {root}" label. So the whole-search record is the one entry in a grep's fold that has a label and no output of its own.

Nothing in this function bounds what it returns, and nothing in it records that anything downstream did.

The census block is introduced by a comment reading "what a modification-target census cannot see", and explains itself: "The census refusal is textual and rooted, and each of these is a way a use of a symbol escapes a textual search or a way a found site still tells you nothing. Printed rather than left implicit, because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed."

The line the ticket quotes is there verbatim: "whatever the platform's grep skipped — symlinked directories and binary files bound what a whole-worktree search physically visited". Its two named causes are both platform accidents — symlinked directories and binary files — and its verb is "skipped", with no notion of anything tetel itself chose not to visit. Every entry in this list is a static string; nothing in the list is per-search or parameterised.

Two things about refusing rather than reporting a bound in `look_grep`.

(1) The ordering does NOT force report-over-refuse. In the match branch (src/observe.rs:438-478) `printed.push_str(&stdout)` and the exclusion note run FIRST, before `by_file` is built and before any `PendingEntry` is constructed; the `Search` entry and the per-file `GrepMatch` entries are pushed onto the in-memory `buf` after that, and `pending::save(workspace_dir, &buf)?` is the last statement before `Ok(LookOutcome { printed })`. So an implementation that bounds while assembling `printed` reaches the bound before any entry exists and before anything is persisted, and could return `Err` there discarding nothing. Nothing in this range makes a refusal impossible.

(2) What does decide it is the crate's own report-versus-refuse discriminator, stated in `targets.rs`'s module doc (targets.rs:44-49): the census refusal is a refusal because "Here nothing is left to tell: the remedy is singular. Run the workspace-rooted grep, mint the fact, cite it — or withdraw the target", as against `scope`, which "stayed human-owed because only a person can tell context from conclusion". A whole-`src` grep for `refuse` shows every `workspace::refuse` call site in the crate is of that singular-remedy kind — a missing or malformed input, or a forbidden flag combination: claims.rs (no --proposition, no such claim, --revise without --why, unknown cited fact), facts.rs (empty note, no such fact), prose.rs (--ack combined with any of --text/--revise/--heading/--level/--cites/--before, --level out of 1..=6), targets.rs (no symbol, uncensused symbol), transplants.rs (empty --text, withdrawn ids, an unanswered premise at render), observe.rs (no such path, invalid --lines range, `--grep` without a path, `lines` with `grep`). Not one refusal anywhere in src is keyed to the size or content of a result. A byte budget is not a singular-remedy condition: the author who hits it has no act that re-runs the search under the budget.

What a label change actually costs, in `facts::mint` (src/facts.rs:400-435). The fact's `extent` is built by copying each pending entry's `key`, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `kind`, `pattern` and `out_len` — so the label IS the extent's label, verbatim. The pin is then `sha256:` over a string assembled by pushing, for every entry in buffer order, `label` + '
' + `world_root` + '
' + `world_state` + '
' + `output` + '
'; its own comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker". So altering an entry's label alters both the extent bytes and the pin, and both are carried in the `FactEvent::Create` this function builds and persists. A bound that adds a segment to a label therefore does change the extent and the pin on exactly the observations where it bites; what it leaves untouched is `output` (the captured bytes), `key`, `world_root` and `world_state`. Also visible here: `out_len: Some(e.output.len())` — the extent already carries a length derived from the captured output, so storing a measurement alongside an observation is not foreign to this record type.

records.text: Two things that together make the zero-content case reachable and make a `look_path` shortfall recomputable from shipped bytes. (1) `look_path` (src/observe.rs:277-300) refuses exactly two conditions — a path that does not exist, and a directory — and then does `fs::read_to_string(p)` on whatever remains. No exclusion filtering is applied on this path at all: the only construction of `Exclusions` in the module is `Exclusions::decide(root_path)` at observe.rs:389, inside `look_grep`, and `decide` itself returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any root that is not a directory. So a tracked path under a `.tetel/` snapshot directory is opened by `look <path>` like any other file, and the four long-line ledgers are reachable. (2) `snapshot.rs`'s `SNAPSHOT_FILES` (src/snapshot.rs:71-100) is a ten-entry enumeration whose first element is `facts.jsonl`, so every fact's persisted `output` — for a `Path` entry, the complete selected text — ships beside the rendered memo. The enumeration's own comment says the list is enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that shipping a workspace file is a deliberate decision.

`printed` in `look_grep` is assembled in two separate pushes on the match branch (src/observe.rs:437-439): `printed.push_str(&stdout)` and then `printed.push_str(&format!("({note})\n"))`, where `note` is `exclusion_note(&exclusions)` computed at observe.rs:417. The zero-match branch (observe.rs:421-435) pushes the same `({note})` line after its "no matches" line. So the exclusion note is a distinct trailing segment of `printed`, not part of grep's stdout, and it is present in every return `look_grep` makes. `exclusion_note`'s own doc comment (observe.rs:182-194) states why the text exists: silence about an exclusion is ambiguous between "nothing was hidden" and "nobody said", and the memo paths are listed rather than counted so that two searches over different memo sets do not fingerprint identically. That doc comment locates the text in the whole-search record's `label`; the code at 437-439 shows it is also pushed into the author-facing return. A budget applied to the `stdout` portion alone therefore leaves the note intact in the return, while a budget applied to the assembled `printed` could cut the note off the author-facing surface.

What `look_path` selects and what it wraps that selection in, read at src/observe.rs:277-337 for the purpose of settling the budget's referent on the path side. (1) The selected text is `shown`: with no `--lines` it is `contents.clone()`, the whole file; with `--lines a:b` it is `all[a - 1..end].join("
")` over `contents.lines()`, where `end = b.min(total)` — so the selection is 1-based, begins at line `a`, and is joined without a trailing newline. (2) `printed` is a separate `String::new()` assembled in up to three pushes: `printed.push_str(&format!("==> {path} <==
"))`, then `printed.push_str(&shown)`, then a single `'
'` if `shown` is non-empty and does not already end in one. (3) The header therefore exists in `printed` and in no other place: `PendingEntry { output: shown, .. }` receives the selection alone, so neither the header nor the trailing-newline pad is ever part of the captured output, the label, the key or anything that ships in the snapshot. A budget measured over the assembled `printed` would consume the header before any content, and would count `==> ` plus the path plus ` <==
` against the file's own bytes; a budget measured over `shown` counts only what was selected.

Where the floor actually fires, measured over the four tracked files that hold a single line above 32768 bytes, by simulating this design's release rule (accumulate whole lines, counting the `join("\n")` separator between them, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the budget) against each file's per-line byte lengths in order.

The over-budget line is NEVER the first line of any of the four. Positions of the over-budget lines, and what a selection beginning at line 1 — which is exactly what a plain `look <path>` selects — releases:

  tet46 …/facts.jsonl — 20 lines, first line 978 B, over-budget lines at positions 11 (757177 B) and 15 (905745 B). A plain read releases 5 whole lines, 24947 B, stopping before line 6 (8029 B) because the budget is exhausted by ordinary whole lines, not because any line was over budget.
  tet30 …/facts.jsonl — 21 lines, first line 882 B, over-budget line at position 15 (574898 B). A plain read releases 2 whole lines, 11976 B.
  tet29 …/facts.jsonl — 11 lines, first line 1273 B, over-budget line at position 2 (57249 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1273 B.
  tet28 …/facts.jsonl — 10 lines, first line 1237 B, over-budget line at position 2 (34477 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1237 B.

So on all four, a plain `look <path>` returns between 1237 and 24947 bytes of whole lines and the floor does not fire. The floor fires when and only when the FIRST line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four is reachable from exactly five ranges: `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on tet46, `--lines 15:B` on tet30, `--lines 2:B` on tet29 and `--lines 2:B` on tet28 (any B at or past that line). A range that merely contains an over-budget line does not reach the floor and returns no byte of that line: `--lines 12:20` on tet46 releases lines 12-14 (3 whole lines, 11852 B) and stops before line 15; `--lines 8:20` on tet46 releases 3 whole lines, 6608 B; `--lines 12:21` on tet30 releases 3 whole lines, 12855 B.

records.text: `run` has this ticket's defect and this design does not fix it — read so that the standing non-coverage entry can be written honestly about what it does and does not cover. (1) `run_command` (src/observe.rs:537-621) captures the child's merged stdout/stderr into one buffer, converts it with `String::from_utf8_lossy`, and then uses the same value twice: `output: output_text.clone()` into a `PendingEntry` of kind `ObservationKind::Proc` keyed by the command line and labelled `proc: {cmdline} (exit {exit_code})`, and `Ok(RunOutcome { printed: output_text, .. })` as the return. Nothing anywhere in the function measures, bounds or truncates either copy, and the label carries the command line and the exit code and no measure of size. (2) Both front ends hand that return back whole: the CLI does `print!("{}", outcome.printed)` (src/main.rs:526) and the MCP handler returns it as the `"output"` field of a structured result (src/mcp.rs:652-657), neither measuring it. (3) The `run` tool's own description (mcp.rs:649) already contemplates the large case and answers it by warning the author rather than by bounding anything: "The whole output is captured verbatim and, once minted into a fact, becomes permanently unrevisable and ships into the snapshot beside the memo — so a command whose output is enormous, or contains a credential, puts that in a repository forever." So a `run` return overruns the caller's cap exactly as an unbounded `look` return does, and the only thing standing against it today is that warning. Note the census scope here: this fact opens `run_command`, its two call sites and the `run` tool description; it is not a whole-worktree census of any symbol.

`look_grep` is two modes selected by whether its root is a directory, and the single-file mode leaves stdout order recoverable from the shipped ledger. `-r` is pushed only `if root_path.is_dir()` (observe.rs:361-363), and `Exclusions::decide` returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any non-directory root (observe.rs:252-254), so `look --grep <pattern> <one file>` is a first-class mode that searches exactly that file and applies no exclusions. `-H` is pushed unconditionally, so even in that mode every stdout line is `<file>:<lineno>:<text>`. In that mode the `BTreeMap` `by_file` has exactly one key, and its `Vec<String>` holds each matched line's `{lineno}:{text}` in stdout order (the `for line in stdout.lines()` push order), and the shipped `GrepMatch` entry's `output` is `matches.join("\n")` with label `{file} (grep: {pattern})`. So the file name, the line order and every matched line are all in the ledger, and the full grep stdout reconstructs from a single-file `GrepMatch` entry. With a directory root the same map holds many keys ordered by filename, which is not the stdout order.

In `look_path` the label is finished before the string the bound applies to exists — the opposite statement order from `look_grep`. `let (shown, label) = match lines { ... };` completes at observe.rs:297-312 and fixes `label` in all three of its arms (`path.to_string()`, the "nothing in range" form, and `{path} lines {a}-{end}`), and only afterwards, at observe.rs:314, does `let mut printed = String::new()` begin assembling the return. The label is then moved into `PendingEntry { label, .. }` at 321-330 unchanged. So an implementer who bounds `printed` at 316 where `shown` is pushed, and leaves the `match lines` block untouched, gets a cut return with a label that says nothing about the cut, which is the silent cut the design exists to stop. In `look_grep` the same edit is naturally safe: `printed.push_str(&stdout)` at observe.rs:438 opens the match branch and the `Search` label is built afterwards at 457-460.

Working tree pin for this design: branch tet30-prose-revised-since-proof, HEAD c821b94d6e1fbf4dc43a1691c975e440448534d2 ("check: report prose that moved while the claims it cites stood still"), `git status --porcelain -b` shows only the branch line, i.e. no modified, staged or untracked files.

`prose_after_proof` (src/checks.rs, doc comment through the function body) computes, per non-heading prose block with a non-empty current citation list: `first_proof[claim]` = the EARLIEST evidence record whose `proposition_digest` exactly equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition and whose verdict is not `Refutes` (an empty/pre-digest digest does not qualify; `Qualifies` does); `anchor` = the MAX of `first_proof` over those cited claims that have one, with an existential gate `if cited.is_empty() { continue }` skipping the block entirely when no cited claim is in proof; `block_timestamp` = the timestamp of the EARLIEST event in the block's history whose text AND cite-list BOTH equal the current ones (`min_by_key` over `filter(|(_,t,c,_)| t == cur_text && c == cur_cite)`), with that event's own `why` carried alongside. The block is listed iff `block_timestamp > anchor`. Because `first_proof` is a per-claim minimum, the anchor can only rise when a cited claim that previously had NO first proof acquires one; a later record grading a claim already in proof does not move it.

Where a new workspace event can live, tested three ways.

(1) SCHEMA: `ProseEvent` in src/prose.rs carries `#[serde(tag = "event")]` with exactly two variants, `Create` and `Revise`. Both variants' later-added fields (`before` on Create, `cite` on Revise) use `#[serde(default)]` with comments stating "an old log replays exactly as it did" — i.e. field-level forward compatibility is established practice within a variant.

(2) READER: `workspace::read_jsonl` in src/workspace.rs treats a missing file as empty and skips blank lines, but maps ANY line's `serde_json::from_str` failure to `Err(io::Error::InvalidData)` and returns it — the whole log fails, no line is skipped.

(3) EXPERIMENT: I created a scratch workspace `tet61lab` whose prose.jsonl held one valid `{"event":"Create",...}` line followed by one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line, then ran the build at this pin (`cargo run --bin tetel -- query prose --workspace tet61lab`). Output: `tetel: error querying: unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise` at line 1 column 14`, exit 1. So a build that does not know a new tag value cannot read the log AT ALL — including the pre-existing Create line. The scratch workspace was then deleted (`rm -rf`, confirmed absent) and `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.

(4) SNAPSHOT MANIFEST: `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES` in src/snapshot.rs is a `const [&str; 9]` explicitly enumerating the shipped files (facts/claims/prose/targets/transplants .jsonl, counters.json, pending.json, refusals.log, identity.json), with a doc comment saying it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`." The same module's doc comment states "Because `render` is deterministic in the workspace alone, a snapshot either re-renders its memo byte-for-byte or it does not", and commits the project to "a rendered memo is never hand-edited."

TET-30's memo, evidence-ledger rows C4-C11 (docs/design/tet30-prose-revised-since-grounding.md lines 97-104), all marked OWED.

C6 states the clearing story this design must replace: "Two things clear a listing. Reverting the text and citations to what they were when the claims settled, which works because the timestamp is looked up by content rather than by event order even though prose.jsonl is append-only. And revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded, which is the remedy the finding calls for". It then states the cost verbatim: "neither remedy is cheap, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until some claim moves or the edit is undone, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line." C6 also establishes that a further grounding pass over unchanged wording "appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block", and that a citation-only revision lists rather than clears.

C11 states the guarantee this design breaks, verbatim: "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes, nothing is executed and no file the document names is opened." C11 also states "`machine_check_failed` is not touched, which is what makes this human-owed by construction rather than by intention", and that the check's claims must come from the rendered document's imported ledger, never the snapshot's claims.jsonl, because the two sources are not the same string.

C10 states the entry format: bullets in the existing flat human-owed list, one entry per listed block plus one preamble entry carrying the two-clocks caveat; each entry "names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins", "each cited claim, that claim's first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp — the inputs to the comparison, so a reader can disbelieve the conclusion."

C7 states the ordering's bound: the residue compares an authoring workspace's clock against a grounding pass's; the two are the same unit and epoch (UTC seconds, no timezone term), but "What no record establishes is that the two processes kept the same wall clock", and an ordering the line reports "can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof."

C4 states the pair key and that keying on text rather than last event "is what lets a byte-exact revert clear a listing, since prose.jsonl is append-only and a revert can only append a later timestamp", and that clause (b) is existential so a record-less citation cannot suppress a block silently.

C5 states creations count as well as revisions, and closes the evasion whereby a fresh paragraph under already-settled claims would otherwise escape.

records.text: In src/checks.rs, `Findings::machine_check_failed` returns true if any of grammar_errors, subset_failures, abutting_failures, unsettled_failures, cascade_failures, ledger_errors, verdict_disagreements, out_of_proof, uncensused_targets, unquoted_premises is non-empty, or `provenance_failed()`. `prose_revised_since_proof` is declared on `Findings` immediately above this impl and is NOT among them. It is passed in rather than read here so this function stays a pure function of the document it grades — and it is *always* printed, including on the no-rows path, because the whole point is that two outputs which disagree can be told apart by their checker. Nothing binds a rendered memo to the workspace that produced it. src/main.rs lines 820-842: the render arm is `Command::Render { out } => { let workspace_dir = tetel::workspace::workspace_dir(&cli.workspace); ... }` — the workspace comes from the global `--workspace` flag on each invocation, and the destination comes from `out`. There is no lookup of who rendered this path before, no comparison against anything in an existing `<memo>.tetel/`, and no refusal on a mismatch. So `tetel --workspace W1 render --out M` followed later by `tetel --workspace W2 render --out M` is an ordinary, unrefused sequence.

Combined with `snapshot::write`'s copy loop (recorded separately: it copies only `if src.exists()` and never removes), this means the snapshot beside M after the second render holds W2's prose.jsonl, claims.jsonl and identity.json alongside any file W2 does not have that W1 previously wrote — those are left in place untouched. The snapshot's contents are therefore not necessarily the contents of any single workspace.
